TOKYO, Nov 6 : Japan's real wages rose 2.2 per cent in September from a year earlier, marking the ninth consecutive month of gains, government data showed on Friday, supporting the case for the Bank of Japan to keep raising interest rates. • Growth in real, or inflation-adjusted, pay picked up from August's revised 1.6 per cent gain. • Average nominal wages, or total cash earnings, rose 4.6 per cent to 311,409 yen ($1,972.94), the fastest rise since January 1997 and up from August's revised 3.9 per cent growth. • Workers' base salaries, or regular pay, increased 3.7 per cent, roughly in line with the 3.8 per cent gain in August. A labour ministry official cited a steady rise in base salaries this year as a factor behind the improvement in real wages.

It remained below the year-earlier level of 3.4 per cent • Annual core inflation in Japan's capital well exceeded the central bank's 2 per cent target in October, data showed last week, highlighting mounting price pressure and cementing the case for further BOJ rate hikes. • Many analysts expect the next BOJ rate hike as soon as next month. The AI trade imploded on Thursday as investors reassessed their initial, benign reaction to the Democrats' resounding sweep in the US midterm elections, and unleashed a tech sector fire sale on Wall Street. The Nasdaq is firmly in correction territory, down as much as 14 per cent from its all-time high, which was reached only a month ago. Some $2 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq's market cap on Thursday. The question now, of course, is whether this marks a real turning point. Investors on Thursday were clearly gripped by the fear that Democrats will use their control of both houses of Congress to slow the data center buildout. "We are now seeing something of a buyers’ strike in tech. The rubber band could get stretched further to the downside," says Truist's Keith Lerner. And he's in the bullish camp. Tech now looks oversold, and therefore should rebound, right? Maybe, but the market has to find a floor first. Rate a minute A second week jam-packed with central bank rate decisions and policymakers' pronouncements has left investors none the wiser as to the broader policy trend, if there is one. Indeed, it's more likely that policymakers are desperately hoping for more time before deciding on their next steps — slumping oil prices and stock market turmoil will likely cool hawkish tendencies in developed economies, and give doves pause for thought in emerging markets. The Bank of England hiked rates for the first time in three years and the hawkish nature of the vote suggests there's more to come. Australia's hiking cycle, on the other hand, may now be over. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said more data is needed before December's meeting, while two Fed officials said gradual tightening is the best way to combat inflation. It's even murkier in EM — Brazil's central bank paused its rate-cutting cycle and finds itself in a real bind, while Mexico's central bank delivered a surprise "one-time" rate cut in a split vote. A job lot October's US employment data is released on Friday, with economists expecting a net 65,000 rise in non-farm payrolls and an unchanged unemployment rate of 4.2 per cent. Recent labor market data has been surprisingly upbeat, suggesting the feared tsunami of mass layoffs from AI hasn't started. Not yet anyway. US payrolls days are always among the most volatile for financial markets, as traders try and figure out how the data will influence Fed policy. Right now, on the back of Thursday's stock market rout, rates markets aren't fully pricing in another Fed hike until March, and only 40 basis points of tightening in total. Adding in September's 25 bps hike, that's a full hiking cycle of just 65 bps, or only two full quarter-point moves. That would be the mildest hiking cycle in Fed history. TOKYO, Nov 6 : For years, Japanese savers left their cash in bank accounts that paid next to nothing because few things paid much more. With government bonds now yielding four times as much as deposits, that no longer holds and banks are starting to worry. When the Bank of Japan last week declared victory in its near 14-year battle to lift inflation to its 2 per cent target, it closed a long chapter of near-zero interest rates. Now, rising bond yields are making households more sensitive to returns on their money, fuelling a boom in government bond purchases and prompting some to shift a portion of the $7 trillion they hold out of bank deposits. Takashi Kamachi, a 46-year-old self-employed businessman in Osaka, recently moved 600,000 yen ($3,785.01) of his teenage son's gift money, held for years in a Japan Post Bank account, into retail government bonds (JGBs).

"Banks are promoting time deposits again, but I thought government bonds looked far more attractive, perhaps four or five times better in terms of returns," he said. To be sure, the shift is still modest. However, policymakers hope households will eventually play a bigger role in funding Japan's massive budget as stable holders of government debt, and help fill a hole left by the BOJ's diminishing JGB purchases. "Foreign investors can help fill the gap, but what Japan really needs is a stable buyer base, and that means households," said Kenji Nakanishi, a senior ruling party lawmaker and key advocate of expanding retail ownership of government bonds. 'INTEREST RATES EXIST' Retail Japanese government bond sales in the April-October period have nearly doubled from a year earlier to 6 trillion yen. Over last three consecutive months, monthly sales have exceeded 1 trillion yen, as yields on popular retail bonds climbed above 2 per cent, far outstripping bank deposit rates that mostly remain below 1 per cent. "People are starting to realise that interest rates exist," said Takayuki Nakagawa, general manager of retail marketing at SBI Securities, Japan's largest seller of retail government bonds. Many buyers are first-time investors seeking a safe alternative to bank deposits, according to Nakagawa. Drawn by a government guarantee of principal, they represent the same conservative savers banks have traditionally relied on for funding, he said. Despite the BOJ lifting its policy rates, commercial banks have kept deposit rates low to minimise funding costs, offering around 0.5 per cent on one-year deposits, not enough to beat inflation. In contrast, 3- and 5-year retail notes and 10-year floaters all offer coupons above 2 per cent. Japanese households hold roughly 2.50 quadrillion yen in financial assets, according to BOJ data, with cash and deposits accounting for about 1.13 quadrillion yen. Even with that demand, household holdings of government bonds account for less than 1 per cent of their financial assets, compared with roughly 2 per cent for US households' holdings of Treasury securities. JGBs must also compete with global and domestic equities, which have already attracted a steady stream of funds from younger investors seeking higher returns. Eager to find sources of revenue to fund their spending, some lawmakers want to make JGBs more attractive, such as through longer-duration products and incentives such as inheritance-tax benefits. "Now that momentum is finally building, this is exactly the time to give it an extra push," Nakanishi said. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama wants to improve the appeal of retail government bonds. Her ministry, for one, is studying the launch of additional retail bond products, it said on Thursday, while also calling for discussions on preferential tax treatment for buyers. PUSHBACK The idea, however, faces pushback from some lawmakers who fret it would widen income disparity by benefiting already wealthy households. Meanwhile, commercial banks fear a shift into bonds could drain deposits, leaving less ammunition to profit from increasing borrowing demand. Some bank officials say they are already seeing once loyal customers shift money into JGBs. "Preferential treatment for retail government bonds would be a problem," said a senior regional bank official, who requested anonymity. Bank lending has consistently outpaced deposit growth this year, with loans rising 5-6 per cent from a year earlier while deposits grew only around 2 per cent, according to BOJ data, forcing lenders to compete more aggressively for household savings. "A rapid and excessive shift of funds from bank deposits into retail government bonds could weaken the credit-creation function banks are responsible for and affect their ability to supply growth capital to the economy," Mizuho Bank head Masahiko Kato, who is also chair of a banking lobby, said in September. There are also questions about financing Japan's huge debt with household savings. Foreign investors have increased their presence in the JGB market, raising concerns that yields could become more vulnerable to sharp swings in global sentiment. The BOJ's share of the JGB and T-bill market has fallen to 41.2 per cent in June 2026 from a peak of 47.9 per cent in December 2023, as it tapered bond purchases to unwind monetary stimulus. Banks' share has more than halved to 17.8 per cent since 2013, when the BOJ deployed a huge asset-buying scheme. Takero Doi, a professor at Keio University, said instead of boosting retail bond demand, policymakers should focus on reducing government debt. "You could simply end up seeing households replacing banks as buyers of retail government bonds," he said. "That won't solve the underlying problem." ($1 = 158.5200 yen)

(Additional reporting by Takaya Yamaguchi, Noriyuki Hirata, Takahiko Wada and Miho Uranaka; Editing by Sam Holmes)

HONG KONG: China is scrambling to contain a stock market rout only two years after the previous rescue.  Beijing is dusting off the market support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance – informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell. In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48 per cent. THE BLAME GAME So who’s been selling? The blame game has already begun.

Shiva Capital Group, one of China’s biggest hedge funds, has pointed the finger at insurers. In a recent letter to clients, founder Hong Liang accused the insurance firms of piling into technology stocks near their July peak, only to slash positions in late September. The behaviour was “truly baffling”, lamented the prominent investor, who has a large following on the mainland. Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time. China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the United States, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound.  NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness.  That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

Related:

Commentary: Beijing cracks down on cross-border investment but it is up to something grander

Commentary: What China’s underperforming tech stocks say about its real economy

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance, for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2 per cent of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9 per cent in 2025.  Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market – a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.  In recent days, authorities have issued window guidance to several major insurers, requiring them to report their equity holdings, refrain from cutting their losses, and align investment decisions with broader economic goals. WHO WILL BE LEFT TO BLAME? The government now appears to be grappling with an unintended consequence of its own policy.  Insurers may be more patient investors than hedge funds, but they still have to manage risk and meet claims and other liabilities. That limits their ability to sit indefinitely on mounting losses – and can force them to cut exposure during severe market downturns.  Insurers, in other words, cannot be as reliably countercyclical as the “national team”, whose primary purpose is market stabilisation.

Related:

Commentary: China is betting on spreading AI faster than the US can contain it

Commentary: This bad movie is a good guide to China’s stock market

On its latest earnings call, executives at China Pacific Insurance Group acknowledged that equity investing had become “complicated” and that portfolios needed to be managed so market volatility didn’t damage short-term returns. In the third quarter, profits at China’s five major listed insurers plunged, largely because of the decline in domestic stocks. The experience points to an uncomfortable reality: For insurers, reliable dividend payers such as Bank of Jiangsu may ultimately be better suited to their liabilities than capital-intensive chipmakers. Few in China – including Shiva’s Liang – are willing to say publicly that policy missteps themselves may be contributing to poor stock market performance. Instead, blame has fallen on everything from thin liquidity to indiscriminate selling. But that raises a bigger question: Why does China keep suffering stock market routs? Over the past decade, the domestic market has endured at least three bear runs that prompted emergency government bailouts – in 2018, 2024 and now. The next time the PBOC has to put out a fire, who will be left to blame? Foreigners, hedge funds and now even state-owned insurers have all had their turn.

Nov 5 : IREN on Thursday beat quarterly revenue estimates on strong growth in its AI cloud business, sending its shares up more than 4 per cent in volatile extended trading. The AI data center firm said it was pushing back delivery dates for some infrastructure for Microsoft after the software giant requested changes to the network design, though IREN said it would not face financial penalties for delays stemming from those changes. The delays forced IREN to push back part of the timeline for making operational its more than $4 billion annualized run-rate revenue target to January from year-end. The company said the timing could extend to the end of February. The disclosure comes as the Windows maker tightens oversight of data-center projects run by the so-called "neocloud" firms including IREN, Nebius and Nscale amid delays and rising costs, Bloomberg News reported earlier in the day.

Nov 5 : A Siberian burial mound from the ancient Scythian culture dating to 2,800 years ago has yielded the oldest-known evidence for the use of cannabis for its mind-altering effects, with scientists finding its seeds among the grave goods and human hair bearing its chemical signatures inside the tomb. Researchers said the evidence was unearthed in a monumental burial structure, around 460 feet (140 meters) in diameter, located in the Uyuk Valley of Russia's remote Republic of Tyva. The tomb in southern Siberia was the last resting place of high-ranking members of Scythian society, known for its expertise in horseback warfare and gold craftsmanship, and its relatively nomadic lifestyle across the Eurasian steppe. Cannabis is a versatile plant that has been used and domesticated for thousands of years not only for psychoactive purposes — getting high — but also for its fiber and oilseed production. It is one of today's most commonly used intoxicants. But figuring out the history of its psychoactive use has been difficult because of the perishable nature of plant remains."There is a lot of speculation about the use of psychoactive drugs in the past, but very rarely do we find concrete evidence and can actually confirm that a plant was consumed for this purpose," said archaeologist Gino Caspari of the University of Bern in Switzerland and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, who led the study published in the journal Science. "The reason for this is that plant matter and human soft tissue rarely survive, and even rarer is their preservation in the same context. Our study shows the earliest direct evidence of psychoactive cannabis consumption," Caspari said.

This conclusion is underscored by the fact that the discovery comes in the context of a burial site and elaborate funerary rituals. The site predates the oldest previous evidence from the first millennium BC for mind-altering use of cannabis such as evidence of implements in which it was burned from the Middle East and the Pamir Mountains in Central Asia. The researchers recovered more than 1,400 cannabis seeds associated with burials inside the Siberian tomb, and used a scientific dating technique to trace their age to the early 8th century BC. "Things of value in the world of the living often made it into the burial context as an offering in this region," Caspari said. EVIDENCE IN HAIR BRAIDS Chemical analysis of braids of hair from the bodies of several people found in the central burial chamber identified chemical signatures consistent with THC, the psychoactive compound in cannabis, and traces of cannabinol, a compound related to THC. "The human body does build cannabis-related molecules like THC and CBD into the hair. That's how drug tests work," Caspari said. "We cannot really say how they consumed it based on the hair alone, but considering later evidence in the region it seems likely that it was inhaled." The burial mound was constructed using larch tree logs and clay, and the entire assemblage is encased in thousands of tons of stones. The researchers recovered items inside crafted in an artistic form called the Scythian animal style, as well as a number of unusual gold objects. On the mound's surface, Caspari said, the Scythians apparently performed animal sacrifices of dozens of horses and probably also of people, considering the scattered human bones found among the remains. "Finding cannabis in a large burial already indicates that this has to be seen in a ritual context. We have found that both animal and human sacrifices might have been built up on the surface of the mound in the form of a spectral cavalcade. Propped up on stakes, the horses and dead riders would feature as a display of extreme social power within the steppe communities," Caspari said. The Scythians came into contact with rich cultures of their time including ancient Greece, as documented by 5th century BC historian Herodotus. "Herodotus described the spectral cavalcade ritual but we were always quite hesitant to believe his writings, as he tends to drift into the fantastic. After finding the remains in southern Siberia, we know that at least some of his descriptions about the steppe peoples had some truth," Caspari said. The seeds discovered at the site were in a good state of preservation. "This is where it gets even more exciting. We have started sequencing some of the seeds, and we have really well-preserved DNA," Caspari said. "That's even rarer than having plant remains themselves, and it is currently the oldest cannabis DNA known. I think over the coming years we will be able to add details and partially rewrite the domestication history of this important crop."

The FAA said it was proposing changes to definitions of when a flight abort is not mandatory and to clarify requirements and thresholds for when an abort — the early end of a launch or mission because of a problem — must occur. The findings from AI safety nonprofit METR, published on Thursday, offer some of the clearest evidence yet that AI is accelerating its own development, potentially paving the way for recursive self-improvement (RSI), which enables AI systems to build more powerful versions of themselves without human intervention. The 11-week assessment between August and October, which drew on confidential research, interviews and performance data from unreleased models, found Anthropic's benchmark capabilities had been improving 1.9 times faster since October 2025 than previously. "As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025," METR, also known as Model Evaluation and Threat Research, said.

Congress last year approved $12.5 billion to fix the aging US air traffic control system and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wants another $30 billion for additional upgrades as the FAA deals with numerous technology issues. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement.

WASHINGTON, Nov 5 : The United States is warning of an "ongoing cyber threat" to industrial refrigeration systems, saying in a statement issued on Thursday that every organization that depends on cold storage should assume it could fall into the hackers' crosshairs. The statement, which follows a spate of hacks against commercial freezers in the United States and Europe, said that unidentified "malicious cyber actors" were targeting vulnerabilities in internet-accessible electronic temperature and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. Although short on detail about the hackers involved, the statement suggested that the threat to commercial cold storage was ongoing. "If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system," said the statement, which was jointly issued by the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the departments of health, transport and agriculture.

"Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said that the government was "seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally." The government urged operators of industrial refrigeration control systems to pull their devices off the public internet, isolate them from their corporate networks and promptly apply software updates. At least three waves of hacks have hit commercial fridges and freezers in the past few months. Pentagon investigators are treating a series of mysterious malfunctions that hit grocery store refrigeration units on US military bases in August as a cyberattack, Reuters first reported last week. A sweeping hack of French freezers last month dealt tens of millions of euros' worth of damage, while a second wave of hacking affected more than 100 stores across Europe on Monday. The hacks have raised concerns over the ability of hackers to remotely tamper with refrigerators and other critical devices.

Nov 5 : The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Wall Street's industry regulator, said on Thursday it fined Webull Financial $4.2 million for failing to implement programs aimed at preventing illicit finance and other issues. • Between January 2020 and September 2023, the digital brokerage did not implement reasonably designed programs to prevent money laundering and identity theft, FINRA said. • The firm did not have reasonable policies in place, for example, to verify customer identities when they signed up for accounts, FINRA said. • Webull also did not establish policies and procedures to detect and flag suspicious transactions, FINRA said. • The firm also failed to institute a program to make sure customer transactions were done in the best way for the customers, FINRA said. • Webull, which did not admit or deny FINRA's findings, did not respond immediately to requests for comment. • As part of the settlement, Webull has agreed to remediate issues and hire an independent consultant.

Source: Reuters
